title: Here’s Where Our Memories Go as We Age
gist: A University of East Anglia study in Psychology and Aging paints a more nuanced picture of age-related memory change by distinguishing specific episodic memories from repeated categoric ones in young versus older adults.

insights.claim: Memory changes with age even in a healthy brain—recall slows and names, dates, and specific events become harder to retrieve.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline understanding the new study seeks to refine.
insights.locator: Your memory is going to change as you get older

insights.claim: A Psychology and Aging study by University of East Anglia psychologists tested memory in 37 young adults (18-33) and 37 older adults (60-85).
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Documents the study design; small sample sizes temper generalization.

insights.claim: The study distinguished specific episodic memories (a single event) from repeated categoric memories (recurring habits) elicited by cue words, revealing memory loss is more nuanced than a simple decline.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The episodic/categoric distinction offers a more granular lens on which memory types degrade with age.
insights.locator: asked to recount either specific episodic memories or more repeated categoric memories
